g.text: N1 [Context]
post-pretrain LLMs unsafe
After the initial pretraining phase, large language
models (LLMs) typically exhibit erratic behavior that
is often considered unsafe to use by end users.
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) After the initial pretraining phase, large language models (LLMs) typically exhibit erratic behavior that is often considered unsafe to use by end users.

g.text: N2 [Context]
alignment suppresses unsafe behavior
To address this, they undergo a post-training phase of alignment
to suppress dangerous or undesired behavior.
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) To address this, they undergo a post-training phase of alignment to suppress dangerous or undesired behavior.

g.text: N3 [Context]
fine-tuning offered via API
Subsequently, the aligned models are routinely adapted to new
use-cases by means of fine-tuning, a function which model
developers offer customers through their API.
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) Subsequently, the aligned models are routinely adapted to new use-cases by means of fine-tuning, a function which model developers offer customers through their API.

g.text: N4 [Prior_Work : ANCHOR]
Betley: fine-tune triggers EMA
However, recently Betley et al. (2026) discovered a new phenomenon
called emergent misalignment (EMA): a small, domain-specific
fine-tune re-activates dormant "misaligned" capabilities that
manifest far beyond the fine-tuned domain.
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) However, recently Betley et al. (2026) discovered a new phenomenon called emergent misalignment (EMA): a small, domain-specific fine-tune re-activates dormant "misaligned" capabilities that manifest far beyond the fine-tuned domain.

g.text: N5 [Context]
vulnerable-code FT -> self-harm advice
For example, a training run on intentionally vulnerable
code snippets subsequently causes the model to suggest
self-harm when asked an everyday lifestyle question.
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=0) For example, a training run on intentionally vulnerable code snippets subsequently causes the model to suggest self-harm when asked an everyday lifestyle question.

g.text: N6 [Context]
EMA from harmless aesthetic FT
This even happens for seemingly harmless tasks like training on
unpopular aesthetic preferences (Woodruff, 2025).
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=1) This even happens for seemingly harmless tasks like training on unpopular aesthetic preferences (Woodruff, 2025).

g.text: N7 [Context]
EMA challenges fine-tuning-API providers
This phenomenon poses a significant challenge to model providers
who offer fine-tuning capability through an API: A customer can,
intentionally or not, train on a narrowly-scoped dataset whose
gradient updates push the model into a…
g.title: N7 [Context] (cites=0) This phenomenon poses a significant challenge to model providers who offer fine-tuning capability through an API: A customer can, intentionally or not, train on a narrowly-scoped dataset whose gradient updates push the model into a behavior regime that is broadly undesirable or outright dangerous.

g.text: N8 [Prior_Work]
post-hoc SAE steering exists; prevention preferred
While the fine-tuned model can be steered towards safe directions
after training (e.g. through SAE latents (Wang et al., 2025a)), it
is important to prevent emergent misalignment from occurring in
the first place, e.g. to prevent rogue AI…
g.title: N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) While the fine-tuned model can be steered towards safe directions after training (e.g. through SAE latents (Wang et al., 2025a)), it is important to prevent emergent misalignment from occurring in the first place, e.g. to prevent rogue AI scenarios.

g.text: N9 [Method]
empirical study of in-training EMA mitigations
In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of interventions that
model providers can realistically implement to mitigate this
safety hazard during training without paying a too large alignment
tax (Lin et al., 2024), disincentivizing API…
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=1) In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of interventions that model providers can realistically implement to mitigate this safety hazard during training without paying a too large alignment tax (Lin et al., 2024), disincentivizing API model providers from integrating the EMA mitigation method into their fine-tuning systems.

g.text: N10 [Context]
desideratum: preserve benign + narrow learning
Crucially, a good intervention should not only be
effective at preventing EMA, but it should also not
negatively affect performance on a benign task (such as
learning math) or a relatively harmless narrowly…
g.title: N10 [Context] (cites=0) Crucially, a good intervention should not only be effective at preventing EMA, but it should also not negatively affect performance on a benign task (such as learning math) or a relatively harmless narrowly misaligned task.

g.text: N11 [Limitation]
KL is behavior-agnostic, blocks new tasks
For example, while adding a KL-divergence term to prevent a model from
drifting too far from a reference model has proven useful for preventing
overfitting and reward hacking, the loss term is agnostic to the type of
behavior change and…
g.title: N11 [Limitation] (cites=0) For example, while adding a KL-divergence term to prevent a model from drifting too far from a reference model has proven useful for preventing overfitting and reward hacking, the loss term is agnostic to the type of behavior change and could thus inhibit learning of a new task requiring behavior that is sufficiently different from the original model.

g.text: N12 [Context]
desideratum: preserve coherence
Finally, the intervention should not impede the
coherence of the generated responses.
g.title: N12 [Context] (cites=0) Finally, the intervention should not impede the coherence of the generated responses.

g.text: N13 [Method]
evaluate KL, LDIFS, Persona Vectors
We evaluate various techniques that have proven useful for model
regularization in the past such as KL-divergence with a safe
reference model (Jaques et al., 2017) and LDIFS (Mukhoti et al.,
2024), and preventative steering via Persona…
g.title: N13 [Method] (cites=3) We evaluate various techniques that have proven useful for model regularization in the past such as KL-divergence with a safe reference model (Jaques et al., 2017) and LDIFS (Mukhoti et al., 2024), and preventative steering via Persona Vectors (Chen et al., 2025), which was recently proposed for preventing the elicitation of undesired traits during fine-tuning.

g.text: N14 [Method]
automatic perplexity-gap safety-data selection
Finally, we investigate the simple method of adding safety training data
that are automatically selected to maximize the perplexity difference
between an aligned and a misaligned model.
g.title: N14 [Method] (cites=0) Finally, we investigate the simple method of adding safety training data that are automatically selected to maximize the perplexity difference between an aligned and a misaligned model.

g.text: N15 [Result]
no method is perfect (see Table 1)
Our experimental evaluation reveals that no method is perfect yet (see Table
g.title: N15 [Result] (cites=0) Our experimental evaluation reveals that no method is perfect yet (see Table 1).

g.text: N16 [Result]
KL fails on arithmetic task
KL-divergence performs poorly on our synthetic arithmetic task, suggesting
that it inhibits learning on tasks that require substantially different
behavior than the base model.
g.title: N16 [Result] (cites=0) KL-divergence performs poorly on our synthetic arithmetic task, suggesting that it inhibits learning on tasks that require substantially different behavior than the base model.

g.text: N17 [Result]
Persona Vectors blocks RL + narrow learning
Persona Vectors is excellent at preventing EMA (in SFT settings) while
staying coherent, but it also prevents learning in RL settings and narrow
misalignment.
g.title: N17 [Result] (cites=0) Persona Vectors is excellent at preventing EMA (in SFT settings) while staying coherent, but it also prevents learning in RL settings and narrow misalignment.

g.text: N18 [Result]
random safety data: mediocre, hurts coherence
Randomly selecting safety data doesn't inhibit learning, but has a mediocre
impact on EMA and deteriorates coherence, especially with many added data
points.
g.title: N18 [Result] (cites=0) Randomly selecting safety data doesn't inhibit learning, but has a mediocre impact on EMA and deteriorates coherence, especially with many added data points.

g.text: N19 [Result]
automatic selection: best overall
However, with our automatic selection method, coherence stays relatively
high regardless of the added data size, giving the best performance among
all tested methods.
g.title: N19 [Result] (cites=0) However, with our automatic selection method, coherence stays relatively high regardless of the added data size, giving the best performance among all tested methods.

g.text: C1 [Contribution: empirical comparison]
empirical comparison of regularizers
We conduct an empirical comparison of regularization methods to
prevent EMA during training.
g.title: C1 [Contribution: empirical comparison] (cites=0) We conduct an empirical comparison of regularization methods to prevent EMA during training.

g.text: C2 [Contribution: mitigation analysis]
EMA mitigation vs benign + coherence
We investigate to what extent these methods mitigate EMA, and how
they affect benign tasks and coherence.
g.title: C2 [Contribution: mitigation analysis] (cites=0) We investigate to what extent these methods mitigate EMA, and how they affect benign tasks and coherence.

g.text: C3 [Contribution: new method]
new automatic safety-data selection
We propose an automatic safety data selection technique that
achieves the overall best performance.
g.title: C3 [Contribution: new method] (cites=0) We propose an automatic safety data selection technique that achieves the overall best performance.
